Jazz, blues, rock, country, bluegrass, tango, folk music and some film, television and game scores use it too. Symphony and tango use both bowing and plucking; jazz, blues and rock mostly pluck. In the first movement of Shostakovich's Seventh Symphony the cellos and double basses play the same melody one after the other.
低音提琴為弦鳴樂器，歐洲／義大利，四弦定弦 E1、A1、D2、G2，實際音高比記: The double bass is a chordophone from Europe / Italy, its four strings tuned E1, A1, D2, G2, sounding an octave below written pitch, with a fifth string possible down to C1. It is the only modern bowed instrument tuned in fourths, unlike the fifths of the other bowed instruments. In its lowest register the tone is heavy when played forcefully and softer when played quietly; the timbre can be changed by bowing, plucking, vibrato and different bow strokes. Compared with the cello it provides a lower, fuller bass part, while the cello is clearer and more agile.
低音提琴的源流仍有爭議，但常被視為15世紀歐洲維奧爾琴家族中維奧隆尼的後裔。16: The double bass's origins are still debated, but it is usually seen as a descendant of the violone of the fifteenth-century European viol family. Italian sources of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries used violone as a general term for the viol family, and sometimes for the bass viol specifically. Its sloping shoulders and other features keep viol characteristics; before the twentieth century three strings were common, and the instrument later developed four or five, with professional orchestras in recent years adopting the added fifth string. In the nineteenth century Dragonetti extended its solo capabilities, which is why Beethoven wrote difficult passages for it; Bottesini carried Paganini-style violin technique over to the double bass; in the twentieth century Koussevitzky and others raised the standard of solo playing.

The double bass is a chordophone from Europe / Italy, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322-71, and the largest, lowest-pitched bowed string instrument of the modern symphony orchestra. Its construction lies between the viol and the violin family, and it usually has four or five strings, the standard four tuned in fourths as E1, A1, D2, G2, sounding an octave below written pitch. Playing methods include bowing, plucking, and the slapping of some rock and rockabilly styles. It is used in symphony orchestras, wind bands, concertos, as a solo instrument and in chamber music, and also appears in jazz, blues, rock, country, tango and folk music.
演奏者站立或坐高凳，琴身斜靠身體並略向內轉，使四條弦易於觸及；斜削琴肩有利高把位: The player stands or sits on a high stool, the body leaning against the player and turned slightly inward so that the four strings are easy to reach; the sloping shoulders help in the higher positions. Sound is made by bowing or by plucking with the fingers, and some rock and rockabilly styles allow slapping; classical music and tango use both arco and pizzicato, while jazz, blues and rockabilly mostly pluck. The bow is held French style, palm down, or German style, palm up. A beginner can start with the four strings tuned in fourths G2, D2, A1, E1, written an octave higher than it sounds and sounding an octave below written pitch; when a lower note is needed, add a fifth string at C1 or use a tuning device to drop the E1 to C1.
